reader.title: Lynching of Jim Harris
bases: Every report says Jim (or Tom) Harris, a Black man accused of criminally assaulting Mrs. M. Simmons at Vicksburg, was 'lynched', one adding 'by citizens' (A1, A5, A8).

Harris was 'lynched' 'by citizens' after being accused of criminal assault, so he was killed without lawful authority under a pretext of punishing a crime (A1, A5); no report describes a mob or gives its size, so the three-person threshold is implied by the word 'lynched' rather than stated.

All the detailed reports reprint one Vicksburg dispatch, a Picayune special (A1, A2, A3, A8), and the column briefs derive from it (A6, A9, A11); the Mississippi brief (A5) agrees on the core event but may also rest on the wire, so independent confirmation is not established.

summary.text: The lynching of Jim Harris took place at Vicksburg, Mississippi, on the night of April 30, 1888, when Harris, a Black man accused of criminally assaulting a woman named Mrs. M. Simmons, was killed the night after the alleged assault.
The case reached papers across the country only as a brief wire item, usually paired with the lynching of Henry Pope at Summerville, Georgia, the same night.

According to a special dispatch from Vicksburg to the New Orleans Picayune, Harris, described as "colored," was accused of criminally assaulting Mrs. M. Simmons in Vicksburg on Sunday night, April 29.
He was lynched the following night, and the dispatch added that he "refused to confess to the last."
It also reported that he was said to have had two accomplices, but that he "would tell nothing."
The Southern Herald of Liberty, Mississippi, gave the only other substantive version, stating that "a negro named Tom Harris was lynched by citizens at Vicksburg on Monday night last."
None of the reports describes how Harris was taken, whether he had been held by officers, how he was killed, or how many people took part.
No report of an inquest, of any arrest of the lynchers, or of action against the two alleged accomplices appears in the coverage.
Eastern dailies printed the Vicksburg dispatch on May 1 and 2 under heads such as "Lynched for Criminal Assault" and "Lynched.," stating the assault as fact.

The Alexandria Gazette set it directly above the Atlanta dispatch on Pope, and the Barton County Democrat of Great Bend, Kansas, ran both under "Negro Lynchings," with the Vicksburg item labeled "Another Case."
The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer condensed the dispatch into a single sentence and misplaced Vicksburg in Virginia.
Weekly news summaries in Minnesota and Dakota carried a one-line notice through late May, dating the lynching "on the 1st," the dispatch's dateline.

In "The South" columns of Kansas weeklies the story lost its names: two "negroes" charged with "outrage" were said to have been lynched on the night of the 30th, one at Summerville and one at "Silons, Miss."
That place name matches the misprint "Mrs. M. Silons" in one Kansas version of the wire.
The wire and the papers that reprinted it named the victim Jim Harris, while the Liberty Southern Herald called him Tom Harris.
The complainant appears as Mrs. M. Simmons in nearly every printing and as Mrs. M. Silons in one, the source of the "Silons" place name in later briefs.

accounts.label: Vicksburg wire (Picayune special)
accounts.gist: Jim Harris, colored, who 'criminally assaulted' Mrs. M. Simmons on Sunday night, was lynched the next night; he refused to confess and would not name two alleged accomplices.

accounts.label: Mississippi weekly
accounts.gist: A negro named Tom Harris was lynched by citizens at Vicksburg on Monday night.

accounts.label: Kansas column briefs
accounts.gist: Two negroes charged with outrage were lynched on the night of the 30th, one at Summerville, Ga., and one at 'Silons, Miss.'

framing.detail: Papers ran the dispatch as a short item headed 'Lynched for Criminal Assault' or 'Lynched.', stating the assault as fact and adding that Harris refused to confess.
A Kansas paper grouped it with the Pope case under 'Negro Lynchings' and 'Another Case', and regional columns reduced both to one sentence about two negroes 'charged with outrage'.
The Liberty, Miss., Southern Herald gave a one-line notice that he was lynched 'by citizens', without comment.

conflicts.note: The wire, printed in many papers, says Jim; only the Mississippi weekly says Tom.

'Silons' matches the complainant's name as printed in one Kansas version of the wire ('Mrs. M. Silons', A8), and the column briefs pair it with the same Summerville case, so it is a garble of the Vicksburg item; 'Va.' is a misprint.

conflicts.note: Weekly summaries (reprints A6, A10, A12) date it 'on the 1st', the dateline of the dispatch; the dispatch itself places the lynching the night before.
Simmons appears in nearly every printing.

record_check.dossier: Vicksburg; 'Silons' is a garbled form of the complainant's name (Mrs. M. Simmons/'Silons').
No county is named in the coverage.
Jim Harris (Tom Harris in one Mississippi brief).
Accused of criminally assaulting Mrs. M. Simmons on Sunday night, April 29.
Probable lynching: killed illegally on a crime accusation; group size not stated.

record_check.record: One Negro was lynched at Silons, Miss., charged with outrage, on the same night as the Summerville, Ga., lynchings.
record_check.dossier: Jim Harris was lynched at Vicksburg, Miss., on the night of April 30, 1888, accused of criminally assaulting Mrs. M. Simmons; the same night Henry Pope (one man) was taken from jail and hanged at Summerville, Ga.

info: Lynched the night of Monday, April 30, 1888 ('last night' in a May 1 dispatch; 'Monday night last' in a May 5 weekly; 'night of the 30th' in column briefs); weekly summaries say 'on the 1st'.
Vicksburg, Mississippi ('Silons, Miss.' in some column briefs is a garbling of the complainant's name).
Jim Harris, 'colored' (one Mississippi brief names him Tom Harris).
Accused of criminally assaulting Mrs. M. Simmons at Vicksburg on Sunday night, April 29; column briefs say 'charged with outrage'.
Unnamed; one Mississippi weekly says he was lynched 'by citizens'.

sources.note: Fullest version: New Orleans dispatch citing a Picayune special from Vicksburg; Harris accused of criminally assaulting Mrs. M. Simmons, lynched 'last night', refused to confess, two accomplices alleged.
quotes: Jim Harris, colored, who criminally assaulted Mrs. M. Simmons, here, Sunday night, was lynched last night. Harris refused to confess to the last.
It is said that he had two accomplices, but he would tell nothing.
